evidence_quotes.quote: The development of sustainable financing mechanisms is therefore imperative to ensure sustainable service provision. This cannot be achieved unless realistic long-term costs are determined.
Ideally, the water tariffs that users pay should cater for future system upgrade, rehabilitation and expansion costs, as well as ongoing O&M costs.
whereby the poorest households receive a government subsidy and pay less for water. The subsidy may be funded entirely by the government or from other users.

This paper presents a systematic approach that can be applied to determine the overall cost of service delivery based on respective cost estimates for operation and maintenance, institutional support, and rehabilitation and expansion.
These costs are based on consultation with government agencies and NGOs in Ghana and are indicative only.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community drinking-water service provision, long-term service sustainability, and tariff affordability in sub-Saharan Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines financing, institutional support, and governance arrangements for rural water services. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it specifically addresses tariff-setting and cost-recovery rules, payment collection rules (reactive financing, monthly household tariffs, pay-as-you-fetch), community cross-subsidy exemptions, and targeted government subsidy structures governing rural water access and affordability.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis. The paper is a methodological/planning tool and narrative policy overview presenting cost-accounting/amortization equations (Equations 1-6) illustrated with indicative component costs from Ghana for a hypothetical 50-household community (Tables 1-4, Boxes 1-2), plus a narrative discussion of community financing and pro-poor subsidy models citing secondary literature. No empirical data collection method, sample, or empirical analysis is reported (exclude E05).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report measured empirical outcomes on household or community access, connection, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; only computes hypothetical monthly household tariffs ($0.30 to $1.07/month plus $4.23/month capital recovery) in worked costing examples.
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, empirical sample/population, or measured exposure-outcome relationship is reported (only a worked costing example for an illustrative community of 50 households / 300 people).

country: Sub-Saharan Africa (illustrative costing examples from Ghana)
exposure: Tariff-setting and cost-recovery rules, community revenue-collection mechanisms, and subsidy structures for rural water supply
rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Harvey 2007, Water Policy 9:373-391). While the paper addresses rural drinking-water service sustainability and tariff/cost-recovery and subsidy rules (satisfying Criteria 1 and 2 under both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), it is a non-empirical planning/costing framework and narrative policy overview. It presents amortization formulas and illustrative tariff hierarchy calculations using indicative India Mark II hand-pump component and institutional support cost estimates from Ghana for a hypothetical 50-household community, alongside a narrative discussion of financing and subsidy options without primary empirical methods, an empirical sample, or measured access/affordability outcomes. Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence).
